title: The crisis of the welfare state
subtitle: A social contract under pressure
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Born after 1945 to protect each citizen from illness, unemployment and old age, the welfare state is today shaken up by aging and globalization.

hero.hook: In 1960, France had 4 workers to finance the retirement of 1 retiree. Today there are only 2 left.

blocks.text: The **Welfare State** designates all the aid that the State provides to citizens to protect them against illness, unemployment or old age. This system was born in its modern form just after the Second World War, as a promise of collective solidarity.

Since the end of the 20th century, this pillar of developed societies has been going through a financing crisis. Aging of the population, globalization, new forms of work: the balance between social protection and the economy is now being called into question all over the world.

sections.title: 1945: the birth of a social contract

blocks.text: In 1942, the British economist William Beveridge published a report which would become seminal: the . Its ambition is to protect each citizen against five major risks: disease, ignorance, unsanitary conditions, idleness and poverty. [[The Beveridge Report (1942)]]

France followed this movement by creating, in 1945, Social Security. This system was born from a political compromise made within the , the organization which united the resistance movements during the war. The State is no longer content with policing or justice: it becomes the guarantor of the well-being of all. [[National Council of Resistance]]
The welfare state was not invented by socialists, but by the conservative German chancellor Otto von Bismarck in 1883. Its goal was strategic: to calm workers to avoid a revolution.

The balance of the post-war years was disrupted by two major developments. The first is demographic: people are living longer and families are having fewer children. This increases health care costs and extends the length of time you receive a pension.

blocks.caption: The aging of the population weighs more heavily on social accounts each year.

blocks.text: In France, there were 4 workers to finance the retirement of a single retiree in the 1960s. Today, this figure has fallen to less than 2. Second development: the rise in unemployment since the oil crises of 1973, and the rise of , these independent and precarious jobs which contribute less to the system while being more exposed to risks. [[gig economy]]

sections.title: Globalization puts the model under pressure

blocks.text: In a globalized economy, businesses and capital can easily move from one country to another. The taxes and contributions necessary to finance social protection are then seen as a handicap compared to countries where work costs less.

An interesting counter-example is that of the Scandinavian countries. Sweden and Denmark maintain a high level of social protection while remaining very competitive. Their secret is called : companies can lay off employees easily, but in exchange employees receive generous unemployment benefits and strong support towards a new job. [[flexicurity]]
Denmark spends around 32% of its GDP on social protection, one of the highest rates in the world, while consistently being ranked among the easiest countries to start a business.

The system of tomorrow must protect against new risks: the uberization of work, the ecological transition, dependency linked to old age. The French reform of 2023, which raised the legal retirement age to 64, shows how difficult these changes are to gain acceptance.

The debate also concerns financing: should we continue to place the bulk of the system on work, at the risk of penalizing employment, or switch to broader financing through taxes, like the  in France, which affects all income and not just wages? [[CSG]]

The welfare state, born in 1945 to protect everyone against illness, unemployment and old age, is weakened by unprecedented demographic aging and by globalization. Its survival will depend on its ability to reinvent itself without losing its promise of solidarity.
